paper_a.title: Parity proofs of the Kochen-Specker theorem based on the Lie algebra E8

metadata.description: Both papers furnish explicit Kochen-Specker (KS) constructions but at dramatically different scales: paper A builds vast 8-dimensional ray-basis systems from the Lie algebra E8 (120 rays, 2025 bases) and enumerates hundreds of parity proofs, with the most compact being 34 rays in 9 bases; paper B exhibits the simplest known qutrit (d=3) KS set with 33 vectors organized into 14 bases. Both prove the same underlying KS theorem via fundamentally different combinatorial/algebraic machinery (E8 root-system symmetries and parity-counting vs Yu-Oh embedding plus color-triple pigeonhole). The match is sparse beyond the shared external scaffolding (KS theorem, KS set / parity-proof concept).

matches.explanation: Both papers cite the same Kochen-Specker theorem of Kochen & Specker (1967). Both nodes are external-origin and reference the identical foundational result. As per origin-aware filtering, this match carries no signal about the A<->B relationship but is recorded for completeness.

Both define an orthonormal basis inside the working ray system: paper A's 'Basis (orthogonal)' is a set of 8 mutually orthogonal rays in R^8, paper B's 'Complete orthogonal basis' is an orthonormal basis of C^d all of whose vectors lie in the KS set. Same conceptual role (the basic combinatorial unit on which the KS condition is imposed) modulo the dimension and field (real R^8 vs complex C^3).

Paper A's 'Parity proof of the KS theorem' (a set of projectors forming an odd number of bases with each projector in an even number of bases) is a specialized combinatorial certificate that proves the KS impossibility. Paper B's 'KS set' definition is the more abstract no-{0,1}-assignment requirement. Every parity proof yields a KS set, but paper B's KS construction is not certified by parity counting (it uses a Yu-Oh + color-triple pigeonhole argument instead). They play the same theoretical role -- the witnessed object that establishes the KS theorem -- via different combinatorial styles.

Each paper's headline construction. Paper A: the most compact 8-dimensional parity proof, 34 rays in 9 bases (32_2 2_4 - 9_8). Paper B: the 33-vector, 14-basis KS set in C^3, the current minimum in dimension three. Both are minimality results for KS certificates, but in incomparable dimensions and using disjoint counting metrics (parity-proof base-count in d=8 vs basis-count in d=3). The match is on rhetorical/conceptual role -- 'smallest KS witness in our setting' -- not on mathematical content.

Both are existence theorems that a particular ray system is a KS set / yields a KS proof: paper A for E7's 63 rays in d=7 via a proof-tree argument, paper B for the 33-vector Cabello set in d=3 via a color-counting / pigeonhole argument. Same theorem-level claim shape (a chosen ray system has no noncontextual {0,1}-assignment), but applied in different dimensions through different proof techniques.

Both are constructive procedures that generate KS-relevant ray systems from a small symmetry / seed structure. Paper A: family-restricted parity-proof search uses E8 symmetries (U,V,W) acting on a seed basis to enumerate bases by triacontagon profile. Paper B: the Weyl-Heisenberg construction acts with X and Z^2 on the Yu-Oh set to generate the 33-vector KS set. Both invoke a generating group on a seed, but the groups, the seed, and the goals differ substantially.
The E8 root system, its 120 rays, and the triacontagonal coordinatization are paper-A-specific algebraic machinery with no counterpart in paper B's qutrit (d=3) construction.

Paper A's 'saturated ray system' notion (a basis table is saturated if all orthogonalities are represented, equivalent to the KS diagram) is not articulated as a separate concept in paper B. Paper B works with explicit basis lists in Fig.~1 instead of a saturation predicate.
Paper A's compact symbol n_{m1}...-B_{k1}... for ray-basis systems (so E8 = 120_135-2025_8) is paper-A-specific notation and has no analogue in paper B.

The A--H letter labels and basis-profile families are paper-A-specific bookkeeping for the 33 triacontagon classes of E8 bases; paper B has no such partition since its 14 bases are too few to motivate it.

The notion of a 'critical' parity proof (one that fails if any single basis is removed) is specific to paper A's parity-proof framework; paper B does not use parity counting and so has no critical-parity concept.
Paper A's Type 1--4 basis taxonomy (by triacontagon profiles AAEEEEHH, AABBEEFF, EEFFGGHH, AABBCCDD, etc.) is internal to the E8 search and has no parallel in paper B.
The 'pseudo KP set' counterexample concept lives inside paper A's d=8 KP-set discussion and has no qutrit analogue in paper B.
E7 and E6 substructures of E8 are part of paper A's algebraic machinery; paper B's d=3 construction uses no such substructure.

All explicit equations used to coordinatize E8 and to specify the generating permutations U, V, W and the general orthogonal-symmetry form T. Paper-A-specific machinery; paper B's coordinate equations (EP469.1--EP469.3, EP469.7) live in a different vector space (C^3 with Weyl-Heisenberg generators) and parametrise an unrelated construction.
Counting result on E8's ray-basis structure (120 rays, 2025 bases, every ray in 135 bases). Paper-A-specific; no qutrit counterpart.
Generation of all 2025 E8 bases from a seed via products of U, V, W. Specific to E8.
Order of the symmetry group of E8 (~6.97 * 10^8). Specific to E8; paper B's Cabello-33 has automorphism group of order 144 (mentioned in RP469.3) but the result is reported, not proved.

Existence and enumeration theorems for parity proofs of Types 1--4 (e.g. 700,326 distinct Type-3 parity proofs; 400+ Type-4 proof types). The whole Type-by-Type catalogue of parity proofs is the heart of paper A and has no counterpart in paper B's single explicit set.
Algorithms for generating the E8 basis table from a seed and for extracting Kernaghan--Peres sets from it. Paper-A-specific construction pipelines.
Parity-proof extraction from a KP set (selecting one basis from each complementary pair plus seed bases). Paper B has no KP-set construction and no parity-counting machinery.
The pseudo-KP-set proposition (a candidate that admits a noncontextual assignment, hence fails to prove KS) is an internal counterexample inside paper A's d=8 discussion.

Open problems on efficient quantum-gate implementation of U, V, W; on the remaining 29 triacontagon profiles of E8; and on KS proofs from complex polytopes. All E8-specific and have no parallel in paper B.

The Yu-Oh 13-vector set is a key structural ingredient of paper B's construction (the Cabello-33 set contains the Yu-Oh set as a subset). Paper A's E8 construction does not embed nor reference Yu-Oh; the d=3 vs d=8 dimension gap precludes a direct correspondence.
State-independent contextuality (SI-C) is the conceptual frame in which paper B contextualises its KS set; paper A does not invoke SI-C as a notion.
The Weyl-Heisenberg generators X, Z in d=3 are paper-B-specific machinery used to construct the 33-vector set from Yu-Oh; paper A uses different orthogonal symmetries (U, V, W) acting on R^8.
SIC-POVMs feature in paper B's structural commentary on the Cabello-33 set (it contains two unitarily inequivalent SIC-POVMs); paper A makes no SIC-POVM claims.
The Majorana representation (depicting d=3 unit vectors as point-pairs on the unit sphere) is a d=3-specific visualization tool used in paper B; it does not transfer to paper A's R^8 setting.
Three-vertex-type partition of the 33 Cabello vertices under the automorphism group is paper-B-specific structural detail.

All paper-B explicit equations: Alice's and Bob's d=3 bases for the 5x9 nonlocal game, the maximally entangled qutrit-qutrit state, and the classical/quantum winning probabilities (44/45 and 1). Paper A does not formulate any nonlocal game and has no parallel equations.

Paper B's color-counting / pigeonhole proof of KS impossibility uses the Yu-Oh constraint plus four orthogonal color triples to derive a contradiction. Paper A's parity proofs use a wholly different counting argument (each projector in an even number of an odd number of bases). The L1 proof match is appropriately listed as 'none'; per L2 rules we omit individual proof_step entries.
The bipartite 5x9 nonlocal game (Alice 5 bases, Bob 9 bases, win iff outputs nonorthogonal) is a paper-B-specific application of the KS set; paper A does not formulate any nonlocal game.

Paper B's qutrit-qutrit perfect quantum strategy (shared maximally entangled state plus projective measurement in the assigned basis) is an experimental/protocol-level use of the KS set with no parallel in paper A's purely structural / enumerative work.
Refutation of Cabello (2025) Conjecture 2 and minimality-of-|X|x|Y| claim are paper-B-specific consequences of its 33-vector KS set in the bipartite-game framing; paper A makes no such claims.
Uniqueness of the Cabello-33 set up to unitaries is paper-B-specific.
The two unitarily inequivalent SIC-POVMs inside the 33-vector set are paper-B-specific structural observations; paper A does not consider SIC-POVMs.
Conjectures that the simplest qutrit KS set must contain Yu-Oh and that the Cabello-33 reaches the natural lower limit are paper-B-specific minimality conjectures in d=3.
